newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN takes on intervention role in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN takes on intervention role in Cambodia.

text.p: If ASEAN mediates in Cambodia's latest conflict it will fly in the face of the group's oft-stated principle of non-interference in a neighbour's affairs.

Nevertheless ASEAN has long been involved in diplomatic efforts to end Cambodia's civil war and in the 1980s defined itself through staunch opposition to the Vietnamese invasion in 1979 and subsequent occupation of Cambodia.

The group also played an instrumental role in the 1991 Paris Peace Accords that ended the two-decade old civil war, paving the way for elections that brought an unwieldy coalition government to power.
"It seems like most of the ASEAN meetings of the past two decades have been about Cambodia," a Southeast Asian diplomat said.
Cambodia was supposed to join the Association of South East Asian Nations on Wednesday, along with Burma and Laos.

But Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's bloody overthrow on July 6 of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh -- the two were on opposite sides in the civil war -- prompted ASEAN to postpone Cambodia's membership.
Cambodia's Foreign Minister Ung Huot said on Wednesday that Hun Sen had apparently changed his mind and welcomed an ASEAN role in mediating the conflict.
Asian diplomats in Phnom Penh welcomed the Cambodian about-face on mediation, but said they were waiting to hear the premier announce the policy himself.
Three ASEAN foreign ministers -- Indonesia's Ali Alatas, the Philippines' Domingo Siazon and Thailand's Prachuab Chaiyasarn -- discussed the mediation effort with Ung Huot on Wednesday.
The Cambodian initiative comes at a time when politicians, diplomats and intellectuals within ASEAN are calling for the group to take a more interventionist approach to regional affairs.

"As ASEAN becomes more open, as growing interdependence means events in one country can send shock waves throughout the region, we need to rethink some of our most basic assumptions, ranging from the meaning of development and cooperation to the implications of non-intervention," Prachuab told an ASEAN conference of academics, diplomats and businessmen on Wednesday.
Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, in an essay in this week's Newsweek magazine, said ASEAN "must now move from being a largely reactive organisation to one that is proactive".
"We need to 'intervene' before simmering problems erupt into full-blown crises, like the one now unfolding in Cambodia," he wrote.
"We should have nursed the baby, at least through its teething period. That's why we need to consider the idea of constructive intervention," the 49-year-old Anwar said.
But an older generation of ASEAN statesmen, including Anwar's boss Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, 71, and Indonesia's 76-year-old President Suharto might be sceptical.
Wednesday's induction of new members was supposed to cap the group's 30th anniversary this year by having all 10 Southeast Asian countries in the ASEAN fold.

Thirty years ago, when the five original members founded ASEAN at the height of the Vietnam War, the region was a seething cauldron of rebellions, subversion and ethnic strife, when it was believed countries were in danger of falling like dominoes to a Communist juggernaut.
"Every state, without exception, was suspicious of its neighbours," Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi told the ASEAN congress earlier this week.
The credo of non-intervention was borne out of these mutual suspicions and cross-border insurgencies.

It was also a recognition of the widely different forms of government in the group, which now range from a military dictatorship in Burma, to an absolute monarchy in Brunei, a communist one-party state in Vietnam, an authoritarian government dominated by former army officers in Indonesia and free-wheeling democracies in the Philippines and Thailand.
Today, ASEAN groups some of the most successful developing economies in the world. The rebellions have died out. Communist Vietnam and Laos are now members.
But analysts say the group's enlargement poses new problems. It will be far more difficult to reach a decision by consensus -- the modus operandi of a smaller ASEAN.

Noordin Sopie, chairman of Malaysia's Institute of Strategic and International Studies, told the ASEAN congress this week that decisions in the future were more likely to be based on a formula that allows individual members to opt out of any agreement.

The decision over whether to admit Burma -- despite widespread criticism of its human rights record and crackdown on a pro-democracy movement -- and not to admit Cambodia, exposed some of these divisions, diplomats said.

Thailand, the Philippines and Singapore were lukewarm about admitting Burma, diplomats said. On the other hand, Malaysia and Vietnam were keen to admit Cambodia. Still, in both cases the dissenting countries went along with the consensus, they said.
